domain_restrictions: A,B,d are integers with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0
Empty product convention: if d=0 then ∏_{i=1}^0 (...) = 1 so Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1
Assumption: the rational expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) is actually a polynomial, i.e., Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q] (not just a rational function)
Graded ring S is Q[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=B+i for i=1..d
If d=0, interpret S as Q (no variables, hence no f_i witnesses needed)
Each f_i is homogeneous in S with weighted degree deg(f_i)=A+i
Regularity condition: in the successive quotient S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}), the class of f_i is not a zero-divisor (equivalently: (f_1,...,f_d) is a homogeneous regular sequence in S)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let A,B,d ∈ Z with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q_{A,B,d}(q)=∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) with Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1. If Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q], then in the weighted graded polynomial ring S=Q[x_1,...,x_d] (or S=Q if d=0) with deg(x_i)=B+i, there exist homogeneous elements f_1,...,f_d ∈ S such that deg(f_i)=A+i for each i=1..d and for each i the class of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor (so f_1,...,f_d form a homogeneous regular sequence). Consequently, the graded data of S modulo this regular sequence yields the given expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) (as stated in the equivalence).

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.proof_nl:
First suppose d = 0. Then S = k. The only ideals of S are 0 and S; their zero loci in affine 0-space over an algebraic closure are respectively the unique point and the empty set. Since the zero locus is assumed to be exactly the origin, we must have I = 0. Hence S/I = k, which is finite-dimensional.

Now assume d >= 1. Let kbar be an algebraic closure of k, set T = kbar[x_1,...,x_d], and let J be the ideal of T generated by I. Because J is generated by I, it has the same common zero set in kbar^d as I; by hypothesis this zero set is just the origin. By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, any polynomial in T that vanishes on V(J) lies in sqrt(J), equivalently some power of it lies in J. Each coordinate function x_i vanishes at the origin, hence on V(J), so for each i there exists N_i >= 1 with x_i^(N_i) in J.

Claim: J intersect S = I. One inclusion is clear: every element of I lies in J and also in S. For the reverse inclusion, take f in J intersect S. Then f = sum_{nu=1}^r u_nu g_nu for some g_nu in I and u_nu in T. Let W be the k-subspace of kbar spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of the finitely many polynomials u_nu. Choose a k-basis 1 = e_1, e_2, ..., e_m of W. Each u_nu can be written uniquely as u_nu = sum_{j=1}^m e_j h_{nu,j} with h_{nu,j} in S. Therefore
f = sum_{j=1}^m e_j F_j, where F_j := sum_{nu=1}^r h_{nu,j} g_nu is in I.
If sum_{j=1}^m e_j P_j = 0 with P_j in S, then comparing the coefficient of each monomial shows that all P_j = 0, because the e_j are k-linearly independent. Thus such an expression is unique for polynomials in T whose coefficients lie in W. Since f itself lies in S, its coefficients lie in k and therefore in W, and we also have f = e_1 f + sum_{j=2}^m e_j 0. By uniqueness, F_1 = f and F_j = 0 for j >= 2. In particular f lies in I. So J intersect S = I.

Applying the claim to x_i^(N_i) in J intersect S, we get x_i^(N_i) in I for every i.

Now any monomial x_1^(a_1)...x_d^(a_d) with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, since it is divisible by x_i^(N_i). Hence the residue classes of the finitely many monomials x_1^(a_1)...x_d^(a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i span S/I over k. Therefore S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.
payload.role_in_assembly: Turns the geometric zero-locus conclusion into the finite-dimensional quotient needed for the commutative-algebra steps.

payload.statement_nl: Let k be a field, let d be a nonnegative integer, let w_1,...,w_d be positive integers, and let S = k[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=w_i. Let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. If, over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of I in affine d-space is exactly the origin, then S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

dependency_assessment.notes: No forbidden ancestry claims appear to be used. The only dependency issue is the explicit undeclared use of Nullstellensatz.

detailed_findings.finding: The proof correctly reduces to showing that each variable has a power in I, then concludes finite-dimensionality from the finitely many residue classes of monomials with bounded exponents.
The coefficient-basis argument proving J ∩ S = I is valid and avoids needing a separate flatness citation.
The proof explicitly uses Hilbert's Nullstellensatz without a declared/allowed citation.
The weighted grading and homogeneity assumptions are unused; this is not a mathematical problem since the proof establishes a stronger statement, but it may matter for formalization clarity.

result_payload.feedback_for_solver: Keep the present strategy, but make the dependency explicit: either cite an allowed Nullstellensatz result or split off/prove the needed auxiliary fact that for J ⊂ kbar[x_1,...,x_d], if V(J) = {(0,...,0)}, then each coordinate x_i lies in sqrt(J), hence some power x_i^(N_i) lies in J. The rest of the proof, including the explicit argument that J ∩ S = I, is fine.
result_payload.reason: The argument is mathematically complete and proves the stated lemma (indeed a slightly stronger version, since the homogeneity/weight hypotheses are not needed). The base-change step to T = kbar[x_1,...,x_d], the deduction x_i^{N_i} in J from V(J) = {0}, the explicit proof that J ∩ S = I, and the bounded-monomial spanning argument are all sound. However, the proof explicitly relies on Hilbert's Nullstellensatz without any declared or allowed citation, so the dependency side is not clean enough to route directly.
